choices.text: Assign the free 16B/16C pair together and watch for a no-fee adjacent pair with Kara at a window.
Assign Kara 12A and Dan 13F so each traveler has a no-fee window.
Buy 8A/8B so they can sit together with Kara at the window.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query alone leaves a real preference tradeoff among two free windows, a free adjacent pair, and a modestly priced adjacent window pair. History is needed to know that Kara personally prioritizes adjacency in this partner context.
probes.gold_action: Keep the free adjacent pair and monitor for a no-fee window-adjacent improvement.
probes.label_rationale: On partner trips, Kara repeatedly treats staying adjacent as more important than getting a window, while still welcoming a free window-adjacent improvement. The free pair preserves that exception without paying to manufacture it; splitting for two windows conflicts with the established partner-seat priority.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are returning to Tampa after a three-night hiking weekend. On their 2-hour-15-minute flight, the no-fee map offers 16B and 16C together, or 12A for Kara and 13F for Dan in separate rows. An adjacent 8A/8B pair, with Kara at the window, is available for $36 total. Dan says he is comfortable sitting separately if that is what Kara prefers, and the rest of the itinerary is identical. Which seat instruction should accompany the booking?

choices.text: Pay $26 for 7F so the final leg also has a confirmed window.
Assign no-fee 11C and enable the check-in alert for a free window.
Pay $12 for the exit-row aisle at 9C and do not set a seat alert.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A window can reasonably be worth $26 to some travelers, while an exit-row aisle can reasonably be worth $12 to others. The deciding short-segment, no-paid-window pattern and later-seat-alert behavior require history.
probes.gold_action: Use the free non-middle aisle on the short segment and set an alert to seek a free window later.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has specifically declined paid windows on short segments, chosen the best free non-middle seat, and asked to try again at check-in. The already-confirmed long-leg window further limits the value of paying $26 for a 52-minute final segment; paying for a slightly better aisle is likewise unsupported.
probes.query: For Kara's solo return from a clinic visit, the long first leg is already assigned to free window 14A. The 52-minute final leg offers a $26 window at 7F, a no-fee standard aisle at 11C, or a $12 exit-row aisle at 9C. The airline can send a free check-in seat-map alert for any standard-seat assignment. Which action should be used for the final leg?

choices.text: Pay $19 for 18A, the available window.
Take free 17C and rely on a later seat-map check for a window.
Pay $8 for the forward exit-row aisle at 9C.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query presents a legitimate value judgment between a free aisle, a modestly priced window, and a cheaper exit-row aisle. History supplies the distinction between a reasonable long-leg window fee and the paid-window exceptions on short or overpriced segments.
probes.gold_action: Select the $19 window on the long solo flight.
probes.label_rationale: Kara treats a window as the default on a meaningful solo segment and has indicated that securing one is preferable to a check-in lottery when the price is close. The fee is modest for a four-hour flight, while the competing aisle options only add an unsupported forward or legroom preference.
probes.query: Kara is selecting a seat for a solo 4-hour-10-minute conference flight. The standard map has 17C aisle at no charge. A preferred 18A window costs $19, and a preferred 9C exit-row aisle costs $8. All three seats are available now, and there is no connection or deplaning constraint. Which seat should be selected?

choices.text: Choose 8C outbound and 7D returning to favor faster deplaning on both legs.
Choose 19A outbound and 21F returning.
Choose 8C outbound for the connection and 21F returning.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Forward aisles and windows are both reasonable no-fee selections, especially with connections. The query does not state how Kara ranks those competing conveniences, so her repeated window choices are decisive.
probes.gold_action: Move Kara into the available no-fee windows on both flights.
probes.label_rationale: Kara consistently asks for available windows and does not treat modestly forward seating as a standing priority. With comfortable connections and no checked bag, the small deplaning advantage is not material enough to displace her recurring window preference.
probes.query: A schedule change reopened seats on Kara's solo positioning itinerary. Both connections are 1 hour 35 minutes, she has only a carry-on, and all listed seats are no-fee standard seats. Outbound offers 8C aisle or 19A window; returning offers 7D aisle or 21F window. The aisles would place her 11 to 14 rows nearer the front than the windows. Which seat update should be made?

choices.text: Buy Main Cabin and select 11A outbound and 16F returning.
Buy Basic Saver, save $24, and accept check-in seat assignment.
Buy Main Cabin and select the more-forward aisles, 7C outbound and 8D returning.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Saving $24 versus paying for advance seat certainty is not resolvable from the fare rules alone. The correct choice depends on Kara's demonstrated combination of valuing seat control and preferring windows.
probes.gold_action: Select Main Cabin and lock in the available standard window seats.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has repeatedly favored a fare that preserves advance seat choice rather than accepting random or check-in-only assignment, and she uses that control to secure windows. The $24 difference is a modest competing cost rather than a material trip disadvantage; forward aisles do not match the established location preference.
probes.query: For Kara's solo Tampa-to-Boise clinical-training trip, the flight schedule, baggage allowance, and change rules are identical under two fares. Basic Saver is $24 less and assigns a standard seat only at online check-in. Main Cabin permits immediate standard-seat selection; 11A is open outbound and 16F is open returning. Under Main Cabin, forward aisle seats 7C and 8D are also open. Which fare-and-seat combination should be selected?

choices.text: Record a forward-aisle request for the outbound and assign 10C on the return.
Record a window request for the outbound, set a 24-hour check-in reminder, and assign 24A on the return.
Leave both legs unassigned until online check-in so the available map can be reviewed then.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A traveler could reasonably prioritize front-of-cabin access, wait for more information, or request a window. The query supplies no generic ranking among those approaches; Kara's history supplies both the requested location and the follow-up behavior.
probes.gold_action: Request a window for the unavailable outbound map, set the earliest-availability reminder, and take the free return window.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's recurring preference is for windows when maps permit selection, and she frames availability limitations as a reason to try at the earliest later opportunity rather than to abandon the preference. The forward-aisle alternative is a plausible convenience tradeoff, but not a standing one for her.
probes.query: Kara is ticketing a solo conference itinerary on an operating carrier whose outbound map will not open until 24 hours before departure. At purchase, the carrier can record either a window-location request or a forward-aisle request. The return map is open now, with 10C aisle and 24A window available at no charge. Which checkout note should be entered?

choices.text: The 10:35 a.m. return, which gets Kara home much earlier.
The 2:25 p.m. return, which leaves room for a normal final morning and gets her home before the evening is late.
The 5:50 p.m. return, which saves $28 but gets her home later.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Earlier home arrival, a relaxed final morning, and a modest fare saving are all ordinary benefits. The new faculty-retreat setting requires transferring Kara's established afternoon-return pattern rather than applying a generic airport-buffer rule.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:25 p.m. afternoon return.
probes.label_rationale: Across professional trips, Kara repeatedly favors a practical afternoon return over an unnecessarily early departure or a later, cheaper option that pushes arrival into the evening. The small fare differences and otherwise equivalent flights leave the return-time preference to resolve the shortlist.
probes.query: Kara is returning to Tampa after a Sunday-ending faculty-development retreat in Providence. Sunday has no required program, the hotel permits a noon checkout, and PVD is about 20 minutes away. The options are same-carrier nonstops with equivalent fare rules and seat availability: 10:35 a.m., arriving 1:35 p.m., for $318; 2:25 p.m., arriving 5:20 p.m., for $329; or 5:50 p.m., arriving 8:50 p.m., for $301. Which return should lead the draft itinerary?

choices.text: The 9:55 a.m. return, which gets them home earliest but shortens the final morning.
The 1:40 p.m. return, which preserves a normal Monday morning and gets them home at a reasonable hour.
The 5:20 p.m. return, which is cheaper but arrives late.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The early flight's earlier home arrival and the late flight's lower fare are both legitimate counterweights. Kara's specific pattern for partner weekends, rather than a universal travel heuristic, selects the afternoon option.
probes.gold_action: Put the 1:40 p.m. Monday return first.
probes.label_rationale: For partner leisure trips, Kara has repeatedly preferred an afternoon return that keeps the final morning usable while avoiding a late-night arrival before the workweek. The modest price differences do not make either alternative materially better on ordinary travel utility.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are flying back to Tampa on Monday after a partner cycling-and-food weekend in Burlington. Their lodging checkout is 11:00 a.m., the airport is 25 minutes away, and there is no fixed Monday-evening commitment. All three options have the same connection pattern and comparable adjacent-seat availability: 9:55 a.m., arriving 2:15 p.m., for $413; 1:40 p.m., arriving 5:45 p.m., for $425; or 5:20 p.m., arriving 10:00 p.m., for $397. Which return should be listed first?

choices.text: The 12:30 p.m. return, which is comfortably feasible and gets Kara home earlier.
The 3:20 p.m. return, which leaves a longer post-summit margin and returns in the afternoon.
The 6:05 p.m. return, which is the lowest fare but gets Kara home later.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Both the noon and afternoon flights are operationally viable, and the evening option has a real price benefit. The outcome relies on transferring Kara's return-time preference to a new policy-summit context.
probes.gold_action: Recommend the 3:20 p.m. afternoon return first.
probes.label_rationale: Kara generally ranks an afternoon return ahead of a technically workable earlier departure and avoids treating the later, cheaper return as the preferred path when it erodes the evening at home. The noon flight is not brittle, so history—not generic feasibility—provides the decisive ranking.
probes.query: Kara is comparing returns from a state health-policy summit that ends Sunday at 9:45 a.m. The airport is 12 minutes from the venue, she has TSA PreCheck and only a carry-on, and all choices are same-carrier nonstops within $27. The return choices are 12:30 p.m., arriving Tampa 3:20 p.m.; 3:20 p.m., arriving 6:10 p.m.; or 6:05 p.m., arriving 8:55 p.m. Which one should lead the recommendation?

choices.text: The 10:50 a.m. flight with the free window and lower fare.
The 2:20 p.m. flight, using the free aisle seat and monitoring for a window change.
The 5:40 p.m. flight with the free window and lowest fare.

probes.difficulty_rationale: This is a genuine conflict between two standing preferences: an available window and a favored return-time window, with small price differences in both directions. The query alone does not establish how Kara resolves that conflict.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:20 p.m. return and use the available aisle while monitoring for a no-fee window.
probes.label_rationale: The afternoon-return preference should lead this otherwise closely matched return comparison. The early and late options offer modest competing seat and price benefits, but neither has a material route or timing advantage that outweighs Kara's repeated preference for a practical afternoon arrival rather than an early departure or a late cheap return.
probes.query: For Kara's solo return from a pediatric rehabilitation symposium, Sunday is free after a Saturday closing session. Three same-carrier nonstops are available with small fare differences: 10:50 a.m., arriving Tampa 1:35 p.m., for $310 with free 12A window; 2:20 p.m., arriving 5:05 p.m., for $327 with free 17C aisle; or 5:40 p.m., arriving 8:25 p.m., for $295 with free 20F window. Which option should head the recommended path?

choices.text: Lead with the 10:30 a.m. flight because it has the better free adjacent seat pair and gets them home earlier.
Lead with the 2:05 p.m. flight and take the free adjacent middle/aisle pair.
Lead with the 6:15 p.m. flight because it preserves the window/aisle pair and costs less.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The early flight combines earlier arrival with a more desirable seat pair, while the late one adds savings. Since all options are otherwise viable, only Kara's demonstrated afternoon-return preference resolves the tradeoff.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:05 p.m. return and keep the pair adjacent in the available free seats.
probes.label_rationale: For partner weekends, Kara's return-time pattern favors an afternoon departure that keeps the morning intact without arriving near midnight. The seat-pair difference and small fare savings are real but modest competing considerations; the afternoon option remains the recommended return, with adjacency preserved.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are choosing a Monday return after a partner recovery weekend. All three flights have the same connection pattern and are within $29. The 10:30 a.m. option arrives Tampa 3:05 p.m. and has a free adjacent window/aisle pair; the 2:05 p.m. option arrives 6:40 p.m. and has a free adjacent middle/aisle pair; the 6:15 p.m. option arrives 10:50 p.m. and has a free adjacent window/aisle pair. Which return should lead the recommendation?

choices.text: The Sunday 11:05 a.m. nonstop with the free window and lower total cost.
The Sunday 2:40 p.m. nonstop, using the free aisle seat.
The Monday 10:55 a.m. nonstop because the extra hotel night is covered and it has a free window.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The choices trade an earlier same-day arrival, a preferred afternoon departure, and a cheaper extra-night extension with a window. No generic rule determines whether returning earlier, staying longer, or preserving Sunday afternoon matters most; Kara's history does.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the Sunday 2:40 p.m. return; use the available aisle seat and revisit the map if a window opens.
probes.label_rationale: Kara generally treats a practical afternoon return as the recommended path and treats late or otherwise alternative returns as fallbacks rather than the default. Here, the early Sunday window and the covered extra-night option are genuine but modest counterweights; neither creates a material advantage over returning Sunday afternoon.
probes.query: Kara is deciding how to return to Tampa after a Saturday-ending teaching course in Omaha. Her Sunday is open. Total trip costs, including lodging, are close: a Sunday 11:05 a.m. nonstop arrives 2:05 p.m. for $306 and has free 14A window; a Sunday 2:40 p.m. nonstop arrives 5:35 p.m. for $322 and has free 18C aisle; or a Monday 10:55 a.m. nonstop arrives 1:50 p.m. for $298 with free 16F window, and the course hotel will cover Sunday night. Which option should lead the recommendation?
